title: AI All Around Us
subject: AI-Literacy
description: How AI learns from examples: the four-step plant-disease timeline, why correction matters, what data different AI tools need, Arjun's adaptive LearnSpark app, the real Plantix crop-disease app, and how people's choices shape what AI learns.

questions.topic: How AI Learns: The Four Steps
questions.question: When an AI learns to recognise plant diseases from photos, which step happens FIRST?
options: Scientists feed it thousands of labelled plant photos
It studies the patterns of healthy and diseased leaves
It gets corrected after making some early mistakes
It names the disease in a brand-new plant photo
questions.explanation: Learning starts with examples. Scientists first feed the AI thousands of labelled photos of healthy and diseased plants (Step B); only then can it study patterns, be corrected, and finally judge new photos.

questions.topic: How AI Learns: The Four Steps
questions.question: Which step is the LAST one in the plant-disease AI timeline?
options: The AI compares diseased leaves with healthy ones
The AI correctly identifies a disease in a new photo
The AI is corrected and slowly gets more accurate
The AI is given many labelled photos to study
questions.explanation: Step A comes last: after training, the AI sees a new, unknown plant photo and correctly identifies that it has a fungal disease. That is the AI finally doing its job.

questions.topic: How AI Learns: The Four Steps
questions.question: In Step B, what exactly do the scientists give the AI?
options: A few hundred photos of farmers working in their green fields
One perfect close-up photo of a single very sick plant leaf
Thousands of labelled photos of healthy and diseased plants
A printed list of every plant disease together with its cure
questions.explanation: Step B says scientists feed the AI thousands of photos of healthy plants and diseased plants, all labelled. Lots of labelled examples are what the AI learns from.

questions.topic: How AI Learns: The Four Steps
questions.question: The worksheet says the training photos were 'all labelled'. What does labelled mean here?
options: Each photo has the farmer's name written on it
Each photo is numbered from one to a thousand
Each photo is printed in bright colours
Each photo is marked as healthy or diseased
questions.explanation: A label tells the AI the correct answer for that example — this plant is healthy, that one is diseased. Without labels the AI would not know what each photo shows.

questions.topic: How AI Learns: The Four Steps
questions.question: What does the AI do in Step C of the timeline?
options: It studies what a diseased leaf looks like compared to a healthy one
It waters the diseased plants so that they recover quickly
It sends the photos back to the scientists for checking
It deletes photos that are blurry or taken in the dark
questions.explanation: Step C is pattern study: the AI looks for the differences between a diseased leaf and a healthy leaf, such as spots, colour or shape, so it can spot those patterns later.

questions.topic: How AI Learns: The Four Steps
questions.question: Which sentence describes Step D?
options: The AI asks the farmer to say which disease the plant has got
The AI makes mistakes at first, gets corrected, and slowly improves
The AI is switched off until a new set of labelled photos arrives
The AI prints a long report about every plant photo it has seen
questions.explanation: Step D is the practice-and-correction stage: early mistakes are corrected and the AI's accuracy gradually improves.

questions.topic: How AI Learns: The Four Steps
questions.question: Which is the correct order of the four steps?
options: B → D → C → A
C → B → D → A
B → C → D → A
A → B → C → D
questions.explanation: First the AI is fed labelled photos (B), then it studies patterns (C), then it makes mistakes and gets corrected (D), and finally it identifies a disease in a new photo (A).

questions.topic: How AI Learns: The Four Steps
questions.question: Which step shows that the AI is finally doing its real job?
options: Step B, when it receives the labelled photos
Step C, when it studies leaf patterns
Step D, when it is corrected after mistakes
Step A, when it identifies a new photo correctly
questions.explanation: Steps B, C and D are all training. Only in Step A does the AI face a new, unknown photo and give a correct diagnosis — the task it was built for.

questions.topic: How AI Learns: The Four Steps
questions.question: Why must Step C (studying patterns) come AFTER Step B (getting labelled photos)?
options: The AI cannot find patterns before it has examples to study
The scientists need time to print the photos first
Patterns can only be studied after the AI is corrected
The AI must first identify a new photo correctly
questions.explanation: Patterns are found inside examples. Until the AI has been given labelled photos, there is nothing for it to compare, so pattern study has to wait for the data.

questions.topic: How AI Learns: The Four Steps
questions.question: In Step A, which kind of disease does the AI correctly spot in the new photo?
options: Insect damage
A fungal disease
A viral disease
A bacterial disease
questions.explanation: The worksheet says the AI sees a new, unknown plant photo and correctly identifies that it has a fungal disease. The other disease types are not mentioned.

questions.topic: How AI Learns: The Four Steps
questions.question: What is the AI looking for when it compares diseased and healthy leaves?
options: Owners
Seasons
Patterns
Prices
questions.explanation: Step C says the AI studies the patterns — the visible differences that separate a diseased leaf from a healthy one.

questions.topic: How AI Learns: The Four Steps
questions.question: If Step B were skipped completely, what would the AI be missing?
options: A screen to display its answers
A farmer to use the finished app
The internet connection it runs on
The examples it needs to learn from
questions.explanation: Every AI learns from examples. Skipping Step B means no labelled photos, so there would be nothing to study, nothing to be corrected on, and no way to recognise disease later.

questions.topic: How AI Learns: The Four Steps
questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four steps in the worksheet timeline?
options: The AI plants healthy new seeds in the field
The AI studies patterns in healthy and sick leaves
The AI gets corrected when it makes mistakes
The AI identifies a disease in an unknown photo
questions.explanation: The four steps are: feed labelled photos, study patterns, get corrected, identify a new photo. Planting seeds is farm work, not part of how the AI learns.

questions.topic: How AI Learns: The Four Steps
questions.question: Why does the AI need THOUSANDS of photos rather than just a few?
options: Each disease appears in exactly one thousand photos
More examples help it spot the patterns more reliably
The scientists are paid for every photo they upload
The app must fill its memory before it can start
questions.explanation: The worksheet says the more examples an AI studies, the better it becomes. Thousands of photos give it enough variety to learn what disease really looks like.

questions.topic: How AI Learns: The Four Steps
questions.question: What has changed about the AI by the end of Step D?
options: It has memorised every farmer's name
It has become a human plant expert
Its accuracy has gradually improved
It has stopped needing any photos
questions.explanation: Step D says the AI gets corrected and gradually its accuracy improves. It is still an AI that learned from photos — just a much more accurate one.

questions.topic: How AI Learns: The Four Steps
questions.question: A friend says Step D should come before Step C. Why is that wrong?
options: Correction is not really part of how an AI learns anything at all
Step D can only happen after the farmers start using the finished app
The letters D and C must always stay in alphabetical order in a list
The AI must study patterns before it can be tested and corrected
questions.explanation: Mistakes and corrections (D) happen when the AI tries to use the patterns it studied in Step C. It cannot be corrected on something it has not yet learned.

questions.topic: How AI Learns: The Four Steps
questions.question: In the plant-disease timeline, the AI studies patterns to tell a diseased leaf from a healthy one.
questions.explanation: True. Step C is exactly this: the AI studies what a diseased leaf looks like compared to a healthy one.

questions.topic: How AI Learns: The Four Steps
questions.question: The scientists trained the plant-disease AI with only about ten photos.
questions.explanation: False. Step B says the scientists fed the AI thousands of labelled photos of healthy and diseased plants.

questions.topic: How AI Learns: The Four Steps
questions.question: In the final step, the AI identifies a disease in a photo it has already seen during training.
questions.explanation: False. Step A says the AI sees a NEW, unknown plant photo. Recognising disease in something it has never seen is what proves it has learned.

questions.topic: How AI Learns: The Four Steps
questions.question: The plant-disease AI is perfect from the very start and never needs correcting.
questions.explanation: False. Step D says the AI makes mistakes at first and gets corrected; only then does its accuracy gradually improve.

questions.topic: How AI Learns: The Four Steps
questions.question: Which TWO of these happen during the AI's training, BEFORE it is ready to work?
options: Scientists feed it labelled plant photos
It studies patterns in the photos
It diagnoses a brand-new unknown photo
A farmer harvests a healthy crop
questions.explanation: Being fed labelled photos and studying patterns are training stages. Diagnosing a new photo is the AI finally working, and harvesting is the farmer's job, not the AI's learning.

questions.question: Why is Step D (making mistakes and being corrected) important?
options: Corrected mistakes are how the AI gets more accurate
It gives the scientists a break from uploading photos
It makes the AI run much faster on an older phone
It lets the AI decide which farmers may use the app
questions.explanation: The worksheet says the AI makes mistakes at first, gets corrected, and gradually its accuracy improves. Without that feedback it has no way to know what it got wrong.

questions.question: What would most likely happen if the AI was NEVER corrected when it made a mistake?
options: It would become faster but much smaller
It would keep repeating the same mistakes
It would learn the right answer on its own
It would refuse to look at any more photos
questions.explanation: An AI only knows it was wrong when someone corrects it. Without correction it would keep making the same wrong diagnoses and its accuracy would not improve.

questions.question: Who corrects the AI when it makes mistakes during training?
options: The AI corrects itself alone
The weather in Karnataka
People who check its answers
The plants being photographed
questions.explanation: People (such as the scientists) check what the AI said against the true label and correct it. The chapter's opening question reminds us that people's choices shape what AI learns.

questions.question: Step D is most like which everyday learning situation?
options: A student copies all the answers from the back of the textbook
A student never gets any marked homework returned by the teacher
A student skips every practice session and goes straight to the exam
A teacher marks a wrong answer and the student learns from it
questions.explanation: Being corrected after a mistake and improving gradually is just like a teacher marking work so the learner can fix it next time.

questions.question: In the worksheet, which state's farmers use the plant-disease AI?
options: Karnataka
Kerala
Punjab
Gujarat
questions.explanation: Question 1b says the plant-disease AI is used by farmers in Karnataka.

questions.question: Why would a farmer find the AI more useful than asking an expert every time?
options: The AI makes the diseased plant healthy by itself
The AI answers instantly, any time, right from a phone
The AI can also plough the field for the farmer
The AI knows more than every expert in the world
questions.explanation: An expert may be far away or busy, but a phone app can check a photo immediately whenever the farmer needs it — the Plantix box says it diagnoses in seconds.

questions.question: An expert lives far from the farmer's village. How does the AI help with that problem?
options: It calls the expert and books a visit for next month
It sends the sick plant to the expert by post
It gives advice on the spot without any travelling
It drives the farmer to the expert's office
questions.explanation: The farmer photographs the plant and gets a diagnosis right there, saving the time and cost of reaching a distant expert.

questions.question: Does the plant-disease AI mean experts are no longer needed at all?
options: Yes — once trained, the AI knows more than any expert
Yes — experts are only needed for animals, not plants
No — the AI only works when an expert is standing beside it
No — experts labelled its training photos and can check hard cases
questions.explanation: The AI learned from photos that experts labelled, and it still makes some mistakes. It saves the farmer from asking an expert every time, but humans remain important.

questions.question: The word 'gradually' in Step D means the AI's accuracy improves…
options: Little by little over time
All at once in one second
Only on the very first day
Only when it rains
questions.explanation: Gradually means slowly, step by step. Each correction makes the AI a little better until it becomes reliable.

questions.question: Which is NOT a reason a Karnataka farmer would prefer the app over asking an expert each time?
options: The farmer can check a plant at any time of day
The app already knew every disease without any training
The app gives a quick answer on the farmer's own phone
The farmer does not have to wait for an expert visit
questions.explanation: The app had to be trained on thousands of labelled photos first — it did not know anything by itself. The other three are genuine advantages for the farmer.

questions.question: What happens to the AI's accuracy as training with correction continues?
options: It stays zero
It becomes random
It improves
It drops
questions.explanation: Step D says the AI's accuracy gradually improves as its mistakes are corrected.

questions.question: Who is the main person helped by the plant-disease AI in the worksheet?
options: The scientist
The teacher
The shopkeeper
The farmer
questions.explanation: The worksheet says the AI is used by farmers in Karnataka, who get help diagnosing plant diseases.

questions.question: A new plant AI gives a wrong answer and nobody tells it. What should we expect next time it sees a similar leaf?
options: It will very likely make the same mistake again
It will have fixed the mistake by itself
It will refuse to answer about leaves
It will ask the farmer for the right answer
questions.explanation: Without correction the AI has no feedback, so the wrong pattern stays. This is exactly why Step D matters.

questions.question: An AI that is never corrected will still improve its accuracy on its own.
questions.explanation: False. The worksheet shows accuracy improves because mistakes get corrected. No correction means no improvement.

questions.question: Being corrected after a mistake helps the AI's accuracy improve gradually.
questions.explanation: True. This is exactly what Step D describes: mistakes, corrections, and gradually better accuracy.

questions.question: The plant-disease AI in the worksheet is used only by farmers living in big cities.
questions.explanation: False. It is used by farmers in Karnataka, and its value is precisely that farmers do not need to reach an expert every time.

questions.question: Asking an expert every single time would be slower for the farmer than checking with the AI.
questions.explanation: True. Experts may be far away or busy, while the app gives an instant answer from the phone — that is why the farmer finds it more useful.

questions.question: Which TWO are good reasons the farmer finds the AI more useful than an expert each time?
options: It gives a quick answer on the spot
No travelling to find an expert is needed
It waters the crops automatically
It sells the harvest at the market
questions.explanation: Speed and convenience are the real advantages. Watering crops and selling harvests are not things the plant-disease AI does.

questions.topic: AI Tools and the Data They Learn From
questions.question: According to the worksheet, what does EVERY AI learn from?
options: The weather
Examples (data)
Rules in a book
Its own dreams
questions.explanation: The worksheet states: 'Every AI learns from examples (data). The more examples it studies, the better it becomes.'

questions.topic: AI Tools and the Data They Learn From
questions.question: What happens when an AI studies MORE examples?
options: It forgets the earlier examples
It stops needing electricity
It becomes better at its job
It becomes slower and confused
questions.explanation: The worksheet says the more examples an AI studies, the better it becomes.

questions.topic: AI Tools and the Data They Learn From
questions.question: What kind of data would a Smart Plant Finder App most likely learn from?
options: Recordings of children reading stories
Movie dialogues in two different languages
Lists of maths questions and answers
Photos of plants labelled with their names
questions.explanation: The Smart Plant Finder identifies plants from photos, so it needs many plant photos each labelled with the plant's name.

questions.topic: AI Tools and the Data They Learn From
questions.question: What kind of data would a Movie Language Converter AI most likely learn from?
options: Sentences and dialogues in two languages
Photos of leaves, flowers and tree bark
Children's maths test scores and grades
Maps of all the cinema halls in a city
questions.explanation: To convert a movie's language, the AI must learn from many pairs of sentences — the same words in both languages.

questions.topic: AI Tools and the Data They Learn From
questions.question: What kind of data would a Reading Skill Checker for Learners most likely learn from?
options: Pictures of healthy plants and sick plants
Recordings of many learners reading aloud
Photos of school libraries and bookshelves
Movie posters printed in different languages
questions.explanation: A reading checker needs examples of reading — recordings of learners reading smoothly or with mistakes — to learn what good and weak reading sound like.

questions.topic: AI Tools and the Data They Learn From
questions.question: How do labelled plant photos help the Smart Plant Finder do its job?
options: It uses the photos as wallpaper for the app screen
It counts the photos to decide how popular a plant is
It matches a new photo to patterns it learned from known plants
It prints the photos and sends them to a botanist
questions.explanation: Just like the plant-disease AI, the finder studies patterns in labelled photos, then compares a new photo to those patterns to name the plant.

questions.topic: AI Tools and the Data They Learn From
questions.question: How does language data help the Movie Language Converter?
options: It learns which actors are most popular in each country
It learns how long each movie should be from start to end
It learns which cinema hall has the most comfortable seats
It learns which words mean the same in both languages
questions.explanation: By studying many matching sentences, the AI learns how an idea is expressed in each language, so it can convert new dialogue.

questions.topic: AI Tools and the Data They Learn From
questions.question: How do reading recordings help the Reading Skill Checker?
options: It learns to tell smooth reading from reading with mistakes
It learns the names and ages of all the learners in the class
It learns which storybooks cost the least money to buy
It learns how to draw all the pictures printed in the storybook
questions.explanation: From many examples of reading, the AI learns patterns of fluent reading and common errors, so it can judge how well a new learner reads and suggest help.

questions.topic: AI Tools and the Data They Learn From
questions.question: Which of these tools would get the LEAST help from a big collection of photos?
options: A flower-naming camera app
Movie Language Converter AI
Smart Plant Finder App
Plant-disease AI for farmers
questions.explanation: A language converter works with words, not pictures. The other three all identify things from photos, so photo data is exactly what they need.

questions.topic: AI Tools and the Data They Learn From
questions.question: Which data would be LEAST useful for training a Reading Skill Checker?
options: Recordings of reading mistakes
Lists of words learners stumble on
Photos of the school building
Recordings of fluent reading
questions.explanation: A reading checker needs examples about reading. Photos of a building tell it nothing about how well someone reads.

questions.topic: AI Tools and the Data They Learn From
questions.question: What other word does the worksheet use for 'examples' that an AI learns from?
options: Rules
Codes
Tests
Data
questions.explanation: The worksheet writes 'examples (data)' — data is the examples an AI studies.

questions.topic: AI Tools and the Data They Learn From
questions.question: A Movie Language Converter was trained only on English movies. What would it probably struggle to do?
options: Convert dialogue into other languages
Play the movie at its normal speed
Show the movie in full colour on screen
Remember the title of the movie it saw
questions.explanation: Without examples of other languages it has no patterns for them. An AI can only learn from the examples it is given.

questions.topic: AI Tools and the Data They Learn From
questions.question: Which TWO AI tools from the chapter both learn mainly from photos?
options: Reading Skill Checker and LearnSpark App
Smart Plant Finder and the plant-disease AI
Movie Language Converter and Reading Skill Checker
LearnSpark App and Movie Language Converter
questions.explanation: Both the plant finder and the plant-disease AI identify plants from photos. The others work with words, speech or maths answers.

questions.topic: AI Tools and the Data They Learn From
questions.question: Which AI tool in the worksheet identifies plants from photos?
options: Reading Skill Checker
LearnSpark App
Smart Plant Finder App
Movie Language Converter
questions.explanation: The worksheet table describes the Smart Plant Finder App as a tool that identifies plants from photos.

questions.topic: AI Tools and the Data They Learn From
questions.question: An AI that studied only a FEW examples will most likely be…
options: Exactly as accurate as one that studied many
More accurate because it is less confused
Unable to switch on at all
Less accurate than one that studied many
questions.explanation: The worksheet links examples to quality: the more examples an AI studies, the better it becomes. Few examples mean weaker learning.

questions.topic: AI Tools and the Data They Learn From
questions.question: A Reading Skill Checker gives feedback to learners. Which is the best description of what it learned to do?
options: Judge how well someone reads, so it can suggest help
Read the story aloud in the learner's place
Choose which storybook the library should buy
Translate the story into another language
questions.explanation: Its job is checking reading skill for learners, which means recognising good and weak reading from the examples it studied.

questions.topic: AI Tools and the Data They Learn From
questions.question: The Reading Skill Checker would learn best from movie subtitles.
questions.explanation: False. It checks how learners read, so it needs examples of learners reading — not movie subtitles, which suit a language converter.

questions.topic: AI Tools and the Data They Learn From
questions.question: The more examples an AI studies, the better it becomes.
questions.explanation: True. This is a direct statement from the worksheet about how every AI learns.

questions.topic: AI Tools and the Data They Learn From
questions.question: A Smart Plant Finder could be trained using photos labelled with plant names.
questions.explanation: True. Labelled photos are exactly the kind of data a photo-based identifier needs, just like the plant-disease AI in Question 1.

questions.topic: AI Tools and the Data They Learn From
questions.question: Different AI tools can learn from the same kind of data no matter what job they do.
questions.explanation: False. The worksheet table shows each tool needs data that matches its job — photos for a plant finder, language pairs for a converter, reading recordings for a reading checker.

questions.topic: AI Tools and the Data They Learn From
questions.question: Which TWO would help a Smart Plant Finder learn its job?
options: Photos of leaves labelled with plant names
Photos of flowers labelled with plant names
Recordings of birds singing at dawn
A list of popular movie titles
questions.explanation: A plant finder needs labelled plant photos of all kinds. Bird songs and movie titles have nothing to do with recognising plants.

questions.topic: AI Tools and the Data They Learn From
questions.question: Which TWO tools from the worksheet work mainly with language (spoken or written words)?
options: Movie Language Converter AI
Reading Skill Checker for Learners
Smart Plant Finder App
Plant-disease AI for farmers
questions.explanation: Converting a movie's language and checking reading are both about words. The two plant tools work with photos.

questions.question: In which city does Arjun live?
options: Kochi
Pune
Delhi
Mysuru
questions.explanation: The worksheet introduces Arjun as a Grade 4 learner in Pune.

questions.question: What does Arjun practise on the LearnSpark App?
options: Science
Drawing
Maths
Hindi
questions.explanation: Arjun practises maths every evening on LearnSpark; the first questions are easy multiplication.

questions.question: What kind of questions did LearnSpark give Arjun at first?
options: Hard division word problems
Spelling tests in English
Science puzzles about plants
Easy multiplication questions
questions.explanation: The app starts with easy multiplication questions and only later makes them harder.

questions.question: What does the app do when Arjun gets answers WRONG?
options: It shows easier questions again
It gives him even harder ones
It closes for the rest of the day
It sends a message to his teacher
questions.explanation: The worksheet says when he gets answers wrong, the app shows easier ones again.

questions.question: What does the app do when Arjun answers CORRECTLY?
options: It gives him an easier question instead
It moves him to more challenging problems
It repeats the exact same question again
It switches him over to an English lesson
questions.explanation: When he answers correctly, the app moves him to more challenging problems.

questions.question: Worksheet Q3a: what is the AI in LearnSpark doing to Arjun's questions over time?
options: Letting an office teacher choose each one
Repeating the same questions in a fixed order
Adjusting difficulty based on how he performs
Randomly making them harder just for fun
questions.explanation: The best answer is that the app adjusts difficulty based on Arjun's performance. Questions get harder after correct answers and easier after wrong ones — that is learning his level.

questions.question: Why is 'a teacher at LearnSpark's office is choosing questions for him' NOT the best answer?
options: Teachers are not allowed to work for learning apps based in Pune
A teacher would only ever choose easy questions for a Grade 4 child
His sister would then have to get exactly the same questions as him
The changes follow each answer instantly, with no person picking
questions.explanation: The app reacts to every answer Arjun gives, right away, for him and his sister separately. That is a learning program at work, not a person picking questions one by one.

questions.question: Why is 'randomly making them harder for fun' NOT the best answer?
options: The changes follow his right and wrong answers, so are not random
The app only ever makes the questions easier for him, never harder
Maths practice apps are not allowed to include anything that is fun
The questions never change at all once a learner starts LearnSpark
questions.explanation: Harder after correct, easier after wrong — that is a clear pattern linked to Arjun's answers, the opposite of random.

questions.question: Why does Arjun's sister get different questions on the same app?
options: Girls get different maths questions
The app learns each user's level separately
The app is broken on her phone
She chose a different subject
questions.explanation: The app adjusts to how each person answers. Since she answers differently from Arjun, the app learns a different level for her.

questions.question: What does Arjun's dad think the app is doing?
options: Asking his teacher what to show next
Choosing questions based on the time of day
Learning from how Arjun answers each question
Copying questions from his school textbook
questions.explanation: His dad says, 'Maybe the app learns from how you answer each question.'

questions.question: What is the AI in LearnSpark really 'learning' about Arjun?
options: His favourite colour and his favourite games
The name and address of his school in Pune
How many friends he has in his class
His level — what he is ready to learn next
questions.explanation: Arjun's own question was 'How does the app know what I am ready to learn next?' — the AI is learning his level from his answers.

questions.question: Which grade is Arjun in?
options: Grade 4
Grade 2
Grade 6
Grade 8
questions.explanation: The worksheet calls Arjun a Grade 4 learner in Pune.

questions.question: When does Arjun practise maths on the app?
options: Once a month
Every evening
Only on Sundays
During lunch break
questions.explanation: The worksheet says Arjun practises maths every evening on LearnSpark App.

questions.question: Suppose Arjun suddenly gets many answers wrong in a row. What would LearnSpark most likely do?
options: Give him his sister's questions
Stop asking maths questions
Show him easier questions again
Jump to the hardest questions
questions.explanation: The worksheet rule is clear: wrong answers lead to easier questions, so the app would step back to his comfort level.

questions.question: Which phrase best describes the kind of AI in LearnSpark?
options: It copies questions from a textbook
It picks questions at random
It gives everyone the same test
It adapts the questions to the learner
questions.explanation: Adjusting difficulty to each learner's performance is adapting, or personalising, the practice.

questions.question: After a few days on LearnSpark, Arjun's questions became…
options: Harder
Easier
Shorter
Fewer
questions.explanation: The worksheet says after a few days the questions become harder because he kept answering correctly.

questions.question: Arjun's sister gets exactly the same questions as Arjun on LearnSpark.
questions.explanation: False. The worksheet says she uses the same app but gets different questions, because the app learns each user's level.

questions.question: After a few days on the app, Arjun's questions became harder.
questions.explanation: True. He answered correctly, so the app moved him to more challenging problems.

questions.question: Arjun is a Grade 4 learner in Pune who practises maths every evening.
questions.explanation: True. The worksheet introduces Arjun exactly this way before describing how LearnSpark adjusts his questions.

questions.question: LearnSpark makes questions harder after wrong answers to push Arjun to try more.
questions.explanation: False. It is the other way round: wrong answers lead to easier questions, and correct answers lead to harder ones.

questions.question: Which TWO things change the difficulty of Arjun's next question?
options: Arjun answering correctly
Arjun answering wrongly
The time of the evening
His sister's answers
questions.explanation: The app adjusts to Arjun's own right and wrong answers. His sister's answers shape HER questions, not his.

questions.question: Worksheet Q3b: tick ALL the examples this AI could be learning from.
options: Which questions Arjun got right and wrong
How long Arjun spent on each question
Arjun's favourite colour
How often Arjun uses the app
The brand of Arjun's school bag
questions.explanation: Right/wrong answers, time spent and how often he practises all say something about Arjun's maths learning. His favourite colour and school bag have nothing to do with it.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT useful for LearnSpark to learn Arjun's maths level?
options: How often he uses the app
Arjun's favourite colour
Which questions he got right
How long he took on each one
questions.explanation: Favourite colour says nothing about maths skill. The other three tell the app how Arjun is doing.

questions.question: Why is Arjun's favourite colour useless for the app's job?
options: Arjun changes his favourite colour daily
Colours are only useful for art apps
It has nothing to do with his maths skill
The app cannot display colours
questions.explanation: The app's job is to find his maths level. Only data about how he answers maths questions helps with that.

questions.question: How could 'how long Arjun spent on each question' help the AI?
options: It tells the app what time to send reminders
It lets the app charge his parents per minute
It shows which colour he likes on the screen
It shows which questions he found hard or easy
questions.explanation: A long pause may mean a question was hard even if he eventually got it right — useful for judging his level.

questions.question: In the flow chart, what happens after 'If Arjun gets it right →'?
options: The app gives a harder question
The app gives an easier question
The app ends the session
The app repeats the same question
questions.explanation: Correct answers move Arjun to more challenging problems, so the arrow leads to a harder question.

questions.question: In the flow chart, what happens after 'If Arjun gets it wrong →'?
options: The app switches to English
The app gives an easier question
The app gives a harder question
The app deletes his score
questions.explanation: When he gets answers wrong, the app shows easier ones again.

questions.question: The flow chart ends with 'Over time the AI learns…' — learns what?
options: The names of all of Arjun's classmates
How to solve maths without using any data
Arjun's level and what he is ready for next
Arjun's favourite colour and weekend hobbies
questions.explanation: The whole loop exists so the app can work out what Arjun is ready to learn next — his level.

questions.question: What is the FIRST box in the LearnSpark flow chart?
options: The AI learns his level
The app gives a harder question
The app gives an easier question
Arjun answers a question
questions.explanation: The flow starts with 'Arjun answers a question'; everything else depends on whether that answer is right or wrong.

questions.question: The LearnSpark flow chart is best described as a…
options: Loop that repeats with every question
One-time event that happens only once
List of rules the teacher wrote
Timetable for Arjun's evenings
questions.explanation: Each answer leads to a new question, which leads to another answer — the cycle repeats, and over time the AI learns his level.

questions.question: Which order correctly describes the flow chart?
options: Right or wrong → AI learns level → answer → harder or easier
Answer → right or wrong → harder or easier → AI learns level
AI learns level → answer → harder or easier → right or wrong
Harder or easier → AI learns level → answer → right or wrong
questions.explanation: Arjun answers first; the right/wrong result decides the next question's difficulty; repeating this over time teaches the AI his level.

questions.question: If the app tracks how OFTEN Arjun uses it, what could that tell the AI?
options: What his sister's level is
Which school he goes to
How much practice he is getting
Which colour he likes best
questions.explanation: Frequency of use shows how much he practises, which is useful information about his learning — unlike favourite colour.

questions.question: Arjun's answers are to LearnSpark what ______ are to the plant-disease AI.
options: Local farmers
Fungal spores
Mobile phones
Labelled photos
questions.explanation: Both are the examples (data) each AI learns from: the plant AI studies labelled photos; LearnSpark studies Arjun's answers.

questions.question: Why does the AI need MANY of Arjun's answers before it knows his level?
options: One answer could be luck; many answers show a pattern
The app can only count answers in neat groups of ten
Arjun's dad asked the app to wait for a few days first
The app must first check all of his sister's answers
questions.explanation: Just as the plant AI needs thousands of photos, LearnSpark needs many answers to see a reliable pattern. The worksheet says the change came 'after a few days'.

questions.question: Arjun's favourite colour is one of the examples LearnSpark learns from.
questions.explanation: False. Favourite colour has nothing to do with his maths performance, so it is the distractor in Q3b.

questions.question: Which questions Arjun got right and wrong is an example the app learns from.
questions.explanation: True. His right and wrong answers are the main data the app uses to adjust difficulty.

questions.question: It took a few days of answers before LearnSpark started giving Arjun harder questions.
questions.explanation: True. The worksheet says 'after a few days, the questions become harder' — the AI learns his level over time from many answers, not from one.

questions.question: In the flow chart, a wrong answer leads to an easier question.
questions.explanation: True. 'If Arjun gets it wrong → easier question' is one branch of the flow chart.

questions.question: Which TWO would the app NOT need in order to learn Arjun's maths level?
options: Arjun's favourite colour
The name of Arjun's pet
Which questions he got wrong
How long he spent on each
questions.explanation: Colour and pet names say nothing about maths. Wrong answers and time spent are useful signals of his level.

questions.question: How many photos of sick plants did the Plantix app learn from?
questions.explanation: The box says Plantix learned from 500,000 photos of sick plants.

questions.question: How quickly does Plantix diagnose a crop disease?

In one month
In seconds
In a few hours
questions.explanation: The heading says it now diagnoses crop disease in seconds.

questions.question: Up to what share of global crops is lost every year to pests and diseases?
questions.explanation: The box says up to 40% of global crops are lost annually to pests and diseases.

questions.question: How much does the Plantix smartphone app cost farmers?
options: It is free
One rupee a day
A monthly fee
A yearly fee
questions.explanation: The box describes Plantix as a free smartphone app.

questions.question: What does a farmer do with Plantix to get help?
options: Call an expert through the app
Photograph the affected plant
Type a long description of it
Post a leaf sample to a lab
questions.explanation: Users photograph affected plants and receive an instant diagnosis and treatment advice.

questions.question: What TWO things does Plantix give back to the farmer after a photo?
options: A weather report and a map
A loan and a tractor rental
A diagnosis and treatment advice
A new seed packet and a bill
questions.explanation: The box says users receive instant diagnosis and treatment advice.

questions.question: What accuracy does Plantix achieve?
options: Around 40–50%
Exactly 100%
Around 10–15%
Around 85–90%
questions.explanation: The box says Plantix achieves around 85–90% accuracy.

questions.question: Farmers in which country are especially affected by crop losses, according to the box?
options: India
Brazil
Japan
Kenya
questions.explanation: The text says crop losses greatly affect farmers, especially in India.

questions.question: What does '85–90% accuracy' tell us about Plantix?
options: It only works on 85 to 90 different kinds of plants
It is right most of the time but still makes mistakes
It is right exactly 85 times every single day it is used
It is wrong more often than it is right about diseases
questions.explanation: Out of 100 diagnoses, roughly 85 to 90 are correct — very useful, but not perfect, so a farmer should stay alert for the odd mistake.

questions.question: Plantix says a crop is healthy, but the farmer can clearly see it wilting. What is the wise thing to do?
options: Delete the app at once because it is completely useless
Photograph a different, healthy plant and send that instead
Treat it as a possible mistake and check with an expert
Trust the app completely because it is always right
questions.explanation: With 85–90% accuracy, some answers will be wrong. People stay in charge: a doubtful result is worth checking with a human expert.

questions.question: Why is Plantix able to be so accurate?
options: It was programmed with a single perfect rule
It asks a farmer to confirm every answer
It only diagnoses one type of plant
It was trained on hundreds of thousands of images
questions.explanation: The box says it is powered by AI trained on hundreds of thousands of images — and the more examples an AI studies, the better it becomes.

questions.question: Plantix learned from 500,000 photos of what?
options: Sick plants
Happy farmers
Farm tractors
Rain clouds
questions.explanation: The heading says it learned from 500,000 photos of sick plants — the examples it needed to recognise disease.

questions.question: Which organisation is given as the source of the Plantix information?
options: WHO
GSMA
NASA
ISRO
questions.explanation: The box cites 'GSMA — Detecting and managing crop pests and diseases with AI: Insights from Plantix'.

questions.question: The '500,000 photos' part of the Plantix story matches which step of the worksheet timeline?
options: Step D — being corrected after mistakes
Step C — comparing healthy and sick leaves
Step B — feeding the AI many labelled photos
Step A — identifying a new unknown photo
questions.explanation: Feeding the AI a huge collection of plant photos is the data step, Step B of the timeline.

questions.question: A farmer photographing a wilting plant and getting a diagnosis in seconds matches which timeline step?
options: Step B — scientists feed in labelled photos
Step C — the AI studies leaf patterns
Step D — the AI is corrected after mistakes
Step A — the trained AI identifies a new photo
questions.explanation: The farmer's photo is new and unknown to the AI; giving a correct diagnosis for it is Step A, the AI doing its job.

questions.question: What does the word 'annually' mean in 'crops are lost annually'?
options: Every year
Every day
Every hour
Every decade
questions.explanation: Annually means once a year, so up to 40% of crops are lost each year.

questions.question: Why does losing crops to disease matter so much for farmers in India?
options: Farmers in India do not own smartphones
Lost crops mean lost food and lost income for them
Indian farmers only grow one kind of crop
Diseased crops cannot be photographed
questions.explanation: The box says crop losses greatly affect farmers, especially in India — a damaged crop is their food and earnings.

questions.question: Plantix has been 'successfully tested in multiple countries'. What does that suggest?
options: Each country had to build its very own Plantix app
It was never actually used by any real farmers at all
It learned disease patterns that work in many places
It only works on the plants that grow inside India
questions.explanation: Being tested successfully in many countries shows the patterns it learned from its huge photo collection apply widely, not only in one place.

questions.question: Plantix is 100% accurate at diagnosing crop disease.
questions.explanation: False. The box says it achieves around 85–90% accuracy — very good, but it still makes some mistakes.

questions.question: Plantix has been successfully tested in multiple countries worldwide.
questions.explanation: True. The box states this directly.

questions.question: Farmers must pay a monthly fee to use Plantix.
questions.explanation: False. Plantix is described as a free smartphone app.

questions.question: Up to 40% of the world's crops are lost each year to pests and diseases.
questions.explanation: True. This is the figure given in the Plantix box.

questions.question: Plantix was trained on hundreds of thousands of plant images and still gets some diagnoses wrong.
questions.explanation: True. It learned from 500,000 photos, yet its accuracy is around 85–90%, so a few answers are still mistakes.

questions.question: Which TWO does a farmer receive from Plantix after sending a photo?
options: A diagnosis of the disease
Advice on how to treat it
Free seeds by post
A weather forecast
questions.explanation: The box says users receive instant diagnosis and treatment advice. Seeds and weather are not part of what Plantix offers.

questions.question: The chapter opens with a question: if AI learns from examples people give it, then what shapes what AI learns?
options: The brand of the computer the AI runs on
The weather on the day the AI is trained
The colour of the AI's app icon
People's choices about which examples to give
questions.explanation: Because an AI learns from the examples people provide, the choices people make about those examples decide what the AI ends up knowing.

questions.question: Who decides which examples an AI gets to learn from?
options: People
The AI itself
The plants
Nobody
questions.explanation: People choose, collect and label the examples. The opening question highlights that these choices affect what AI learns.

questions.question: People trained a plant AI using photos of only ONE kind of plant. What is the likely result?
options: It learns the other plants on its own overnight
It struggles to recognise other kinds of plants
It becomes an expert on every plant in the world
It refuses to look at the one plant it learned
questions.explanation: An AI only knows what its examples taught it. Narrow choices by people lead to narrow knowledge in the AI.

questions.question: Some training photos were labelled wrongly — sick plants marked 'healthy'. What happens to the AI?
options: It ignores every photo with a label on it
Nothing changes because labels do not matter
It learns wrong patterns and gives wrong answers
It notices the mistake and fixes the labels itself
questions.explanation: The AI trusts its labels. Wrong labels teach it the wrong thing, so people's careful choices while labelling really matter.

questions.question: Who is mainly responsible for making sure an AI learns well?
options: The AI itself, because it is the one doing the learning
The farmers who use the finished app in their fields
The smartphone that the app is installed on
The people choosing and correcting its examples
questions.explanation: People choose the examples (Step B) and provide the corrections (Step D). The AI can only learn from what people give it.

questions.question: In the comic-strip task, how much does the AI know at the START of its learning journey?

Half of its job
Everything already
Only the farmer's name
questions.explanation: The task says to show the journey 'from having zero knowledge' to getting good at its job.

Who benefits from the AI
How much the AI costs
Which company sells the AI
questions.explanation: The worksheet says: 'Also show who benefits from it.'

WhatsApp, YouTube or Maps
Canva, Freeform or Google Slides
Paint, Excel or Notepad
questions.explanation: The task says to use Canva / Freeform / Google Slides to create the comic strip.

questions.question: Which is the correct order of the AI's learning journey in the comic strip?
options: Good at its job → corrected → mistakes → zero knowledge
Mistakes → zero knowledge → good at its job → corrected
Corrected → good at its job → zero knowledge → mistakes
Zero knowledge → mistakes → corrected → good at its job
questions.explanation: The worksheet lists the stages: zero knowledge, making mistakes, getting corrected, finally getting good at its job.

questions.question: Which comic-strip stage matches Step D of the plant-disease timeline?
options: Getting corrected after mistakes
Starting with zero knowledge
Finally being good at its job
Showing who benefits
questions.explanation: Step D is 'makes mistakes at first, gets corrected, accuracy improves' — the same as the 'making mistakes, getting corrected' part of the comic.

questions.question: The task says you can give the AI 'a face, a name, and a personality'. Why?
options: Because AIs choose their own names while they are trained
To make the comic fun, not because the AI is a person
Because every real AI already has its own face and a name
Because the AI will read the finished comic and enjoy it
questions.explanation: The worksheet says 'make it fun'. A cartoon face is a storytelling trick; the AI is still a program that learns from examples.

questions.question: Whose AI should you pick for the comic strip?
options: One that has not been invented yet
One from a science-fiction movie
One that you or anyone in your family uses
One that only scientists are allowed to use
questions.explanation: The task says: 'Choose any one AI that you or anyone in the family uses.'

questions.question: Which is the BEST choice when people give examples to an AI?
options: A few examples, all of the same kind
Lots of examples with no labels at all
Only examples the AI already got right
Many different, correctly labelled examples
questions.explanation: Variety plus correct labels let the AI learn true patterns; few, narrow or unlabelled examples lead to a weak or mistaken AI.

questions.question: An AI chooses its own training examples with no human involved.
questions.explanation: False. People give the AI its examples; the opening question says people's choices affect what AI learns.

questions.question: People's choices about examples affect what an AI learns.
questions.explanation: True. This is the idea behind the chapter's opening question.

questions.question: The comic strip should show an AI that is perfect from its very first day.
questions.explanation: False. The journey must start from zero knowledge and pass through mistakes and corrections before the AI becomes good at its job.

questions.question: If people give an AI mostly bad examples, the AI can still learn the right thing by itself.
questions.explanation: False. An AI learns from whatever it is given. Bad examples teach bad patterns — that is why people's choices matter.

questions.question: Which TWO things must your comic strip include?
options: The AI making mistakes and being corrected
Who benefits from the AI
The AI's price in rupees
The AI's battery life
questions.explanation: The task asks for the learning journey (mistakes, corrections, getting good) and who benefits. Price and battery life are not part of it.
